commas-1.title: Commas in a list
commas-1.rule: Use commas to separate three or more things in a list. Put the last comma before and or or.
commas-1.example: We saw ducks, geese, and swans.

commas-2.title: Commas with clauses
commas-2.rule: When a sentence starts with a part like When, If, After or Because, put a comma after that part. Put a comma before and, but or so when it joins two complete sentences.
commas-2.example: When the bell rang, we lined up, and Ms. Cruz smiled.

commas-3.title: Commas and colons
commas-3.rule: Put a comma after yes, no or well at the start. Use commas around the name of the person you're talking to. Use a colon before a list when the words before it could be a sentence.
commas-3.example: Yes, Sam, bring three things: a coat, boots, and a snack.

dialogue-1.title: Quotation marks
dialogue-1.rule: Put quotation marks around the exact words someone says. When the speaker comes first, put a comma after said.

dialogue-2.title: Speaker at the end
dialogue-2.rule: When the speaker comes after the words, end the spoken words with a comma inside the quotation marks. A question mark or exclamation point stays.
dialogue-2.example: "I'm hungry," said Max. "Are you ready?" asked Mom.

dialogue-3.title: Split quotations
dialogue-3.rule: When the speaker splits one spoken sentence, use commas on both sides of the speaker and keep going in lowercase. If the speaker comes between two sentences, use a period and a capital letter.
dialogue-3.example: "If it rains," said Ava, "we'll stay in." "It's over," said Kai. "Let's go."

apostrophes-1.title: Owners and contractions
apostrophes-1.rule: Add 's to show that something belongs to one person or thing. An apostrophe also shows where letters are left out: do not becomes don't.
apostrophes-1.example: Maya's bike isn't in the garage.

apostrophes-2.title: More than one owner
apostrophes-2.rule: If a plural word already ends in s, add only an apostrophe. If it doesn't end in s, add 's.
apostrophes-2.example: The girls' team carried the children's books.

apostrophes-3.title: Sound-alike words
apostrophes-3.rule: Words that show ownership never use an apostrophe: its, their, your, whose. The apostrophe words are short for two words: it's = it is, they're = they are, you're = you are, who's = who is.
apostrophes-3.example: It's time for the dog to eat its dinner.

verbs-1.title: Past tense verbs
verbs-1.rule: Most verbs add -ed to tell about the past: walk becomes walked. Some verbs change in their own way: run becomes ran, bring becomes brought, catch becomes caught.
verbs-1.example: Yesterday we ran to the park and caught a frog.

verbs-2.title: Verbs that keep going
verbs-2.rule: Use was or were with an -ing verb for something that kept going in the past. Use am, is or are for right now, and will be for the future.
verbs-2.example: I was eating when the phone rang. Now I am drawing. Tomorrow I will be swimming.

verbs-3.title: Keep the tense steady
verbs-3.rule: When something happens in the past, keep every verb in the past. When it happens now, keep them in the present. Change the tense only when the time really changes.
verbs-3.example: We hiked to the lake, and then we swam until dinner.

agreement-1.title: Subjects and verbs match
agreement-1.rule: One person or thing gets a verb with -s: the dog barks. More than one gets a verb without -s: the dogs bark. I and you use the verb without -s.
agreement-1.example: My brother plays soccer. My sisters play softball.

agreement-2.title: Match in longer sentences
agreement-2.rule: In a sentence with two parts, check each subject with its own verb. Two subjects joined by and are more than one.
agreement-2.example: Kim and Jo ride bikes, but Sam walks.

agreement-3.title: Tricky subjects
agreement-3.rule: Find the real subject. Words like of the crayons can sit between the subject and the verb, but they aren't the subject. Each, everyone and nobody mean one.
agreement-3.example: The box of crayons is on the shelf. Everyone is ready.

pronouns-1.title: Reflexive pronouns
pronouns-1.rule: Use myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves or themselves when the one doing the action also gets the action. Hisself and theirselves aren't used in standard English.
pronouns-1.example: Ben made himself a sandwich, and we helped ourselves to grapes.

pronouns-2.title: Pronouns that match
pronouns-2.rule: A pronoun has to match the word it stands for. For one: he, she, it, his, her, its. For more than one: they, them, their.
pronouns-2.example: The girls packed their bags. Leo zipped his own coat.

pronouns-3.title: Who, which, that, where, when
pronouns-3.rule: Use who for people, which or that for things, whose to show who owns something, where for places and when for times.
pronouns-3.example: The girl who won lives in the town where I was born.

items.hint: When I do something to me, use myself.

items.text: We helped [ourselves|ourself|usselves] to more grapes.
items.hint: When we do something for us, use ourselves.

Pronouns ending in -selves are for more than one. Those ending in -self are for one.

items.text: The girls packed [their|her|its] own bags.
items.hint: The pronoun has to match the word it stands for: one or more than one, he or she.

items.text: The tree lost all of [its|their|it's] leaves.
items.hint: One tree, so use its. It's means it is.

items.text: The girl [who|which] won the race is my cousin.
items.hint: Use who for people.

items.text: This is the house [where|when|who] my dad grew up.
items.hint: Use where for places.

items.text: The book [who|that|where] I borrowed is due Friday.
items.hint: Use that or which for things, and who for people.

items.text: I remember the day [when|where|who] we got our puppy.
items.hint: Use when for times.

items.text: The boy [whose|who's|who] bike was stolen called the police.
items.hint: Use whose to show who owns something. Who's means who is.

items.text: The man [which|who|where] fixed our roof was friendly.
